title: Advice to look thick for tall/wide lifters (best practices & mindset)
summary: Advice for tall or wide-framed lifters: they have more 'real estate' to fill so must be patient, should prioritize compound movements for years over athletics, should not chase strength faster than recovery allows, and should reject short-lifter technique dogma, e.g. trying sumo deadlifts, low-bar squats and wider grips and stances.
claims: Tall and wide lifters have more structure to fill, like a large plot of land, so building a full-looking physique is harder
Think of body parts in terms of length and thickness; the biggest wrists, ankles and knees are usually on tall people
Few fitness YouTubers are over six feet; at 6'4 you are an anomaly and cannot benchmark progress against average-height lifters
An extra inch matters depending on where it is, e.g. a femur an inch longer changes everything
Tall lifters do not progress slower; they may progress faster thanks to better absolute strength potential, but each inch of muscle is diffused over more length
A long-armed lifter may need to add two inches to an arm to get the visual effect a short-armed lifter gets from one
Natural bodybuilding is not a race; a true natural should keep progressing into his 30s and even 40s and testosterone does not crash at 29 without a condition
Tall athletic men often stay in sports too long; every year without compound lifts is size left on the table
Tall lanky lifters' strength often progresses faster than their recovery, which is why tall guys get injured more
Tall lifters should not chase strength records; focus on compounds long term, intense bouts of strength work and get most tonnage from variations and volume
Do not take technique advice from dogmatic shorter lifters; their leverages may not apply to you
Lifters 6'2 and above usually struggle with conventional deadlifts because long torsos force excessive forward lean; even Brian Shaw's hips shoot up
Tall lifters may need wider stances and grips on squat, bench and deadlift; shoulder-width dogma applies to people around 5'7-5'9
Tall lifters should try sumo deadlifts: neutral back, more tonnage, less lumbar damage even if less posterior chain
Tall lifters tend to good-morning their high-bar squats; a low-bar squat keeps the bar closer to midfoot and is more stable
The lower back is extremely strong when stationary; most injuries happen with spinal flexion, so stabilizing it lets the legs do the work
Many tall role models are on PEDs because PEDs give free tonnage and tall people seem to tolerate higher doses
Unlike stocky short lifters who must avoid a fridge look, tall lifters need everything big; wide clavicles give a V-taper but thickness is the issue, solved by squats and deadlifts
exercises: less lumbar stress, more tonnage for long torsos
more stable for tall lifters who good-morning high bar
